\chapter{Review --- Two Endings and One Little A}
\label{ch:repaso-gerundio}
\hlchaptermodality{240}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what is happening now, and mark a person correctly.}

I can say what is happening now, and mark a person correctly.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(review)]{(review)}

\label{lesson:ES-C62-repaso-gerundio}



\begin{quote}
Two endings, three families. (\emph{-ando} for \emph{-ar}; \emph{-iendo} for everything else.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three chants.

\textbf{First.} \emph{Hablando, comiendo, viviendo.} — one form each, no agreement, no persons. The smallest thing this book has asked of you.

\textbf{Second.} \emph{Estoy comiendo.} — \emph{estar} carries the person, the gerund never moves. And it means \textbf{now}: for tomorrow you still say \emph{voy a comer}.

\textbf{Third.} \emph{Veo a María}, but \emph{veo la casa.} — the little \emph{a} in front of a person, and nothing in front of a house.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: both of these are Latin's absence}]
The gerund is what is left of a Latin form after its case endings fell off — which is why it has exactly one shape and agrees with nothing.

The personal \emph{a} is what grew back \textbf{because} case endings fell off. Latin marked the receiving end with an ending; Spanish marks it with a preposition, but only where it matters, which is people.

One rule is a leftover and the other is a repair. Same cause.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three chants, in order
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many gerund endings? (\textbf{Two.})

And which of this chapter's two rules is a \textbf{repair} rather than a leftover? (The \textbf{personal \emph{a}} — it grew to replace a lost ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
